transcript:
[00:00] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Samir from Redwood, AE on the account. We thought today we'd dig into throughput tuning for your on-prem cluster — continuous batching, the scheduler knobs like max_num_seqs, token limits, kv cache behavior, and quantization tradeoffs. Lena from our SE team will lead most of the tech discussion.
[00:32] Aisha: Thanks, Samir. Quick note — Priya might hop on around 10 minutes in, she's in another meeting. Our main goals: reduce tail latency spikes during high concurrent traffic, and lower cost per token. We're running a mixed traffic pattern - sync chat, async summaries, and embeddings for search.
[01:05] Lena: Great. Marco, can you give a quick snapshot of your infra? GPUs, network, and how you're currently routing requests?
[01:18] Marco: Sure. We're on-prem — 8x A100 80GB per rack, Mellanox 200G interconnect, and we use our own k8s cluster with nodepool for inference. Right now each node runs a single model instance with 4 GPUs (mig) and we route via our internal LB. We're seeing high variance when bursts hit; throughput drops and latency spikes.
[01:45] Samir: Thanks. A couple of high-level things — Redwood's continuous batching aims to fill batches by waiting a short micro-window for concurrent sequences, but there are scheduler knobs: max_num_seqs (max sequences per batch), max_tokens_per_batch, queue_wait_ms, and per-worker concurrency limits. Those interact with your model's token-distribution.
[02:12] Dana: Quick question — when you say max_num_seqs, is that sequences or requests? Our prompts vary a lot, sequences often 16-512 tokens.
[02:22] Lena: Good callout. max_num_seqs refers to number of simultaneously batched sequences (requests). If you have short sequences, you can pack many in a single forward and save lots of kernels overhead. But long sequences increase memory and kv cache pressure.
[02:40] Marco: We're seeing KV cache growth — tails of conversations keep the KV cache warm and we hit OOM or eviction, which causes latency blips. Any suggestions?
[02:50] Lena: Yes. Two levers — first, token limits per request (truncation or early stop) to bound kv cache growth. Second, adaptive kv eviction in the runtime: prefer LRU across seq ids or per-client windowing so long-idle clients are trimmed. We recommend enabling prefix/KV sharding and setting max_tokens_per_seq to something like 1024 for chat flows, but this depends on your LF model.
[03:18] Aisha: Model is an open-llm variant — 30B, mostly FP16, we tested 8-bit quant but results were mixed.
[03:27] Samir: Quantization is another tradeoff — 8-bit/4-bit helps throughput and memory but may increase latency per-token if dequantization is expensive or kernels are not optimized. Also, some ops degrade quality for long contexts. We usually recommend starting with 8-bit quant with quantization-aware kernels; then measure per-prompt latency and quality.
[03:54] Marco: Back to batching — our scheduler currently defaults to a fairly high max_num_seqs 64, but we still see empty slots because of skewed seq lengths. Is it better to lower max_num_seqs or use token-based batching?
[04:10] Lena: Token-based batching (max_tokens_per_batch) often yields better packing efficiency with heterogeneous lengths. Example: if you set max_tokens_per_batch to 32k tokens, short requests pack more tightly and long requests get limited so they don't monopolize a batch. Combined with a small queue_wait_ms (e.g., 6-12 ms) you can keep latency bounded while increasing throughput.
[04:35] Dana: There's also the issue of tail latency for single-shot low-latency requests like 1-2 token completions. Batching helps throughput but hurts those.
[04:45] Samir: Right — Redwood supports route-based SLOs: you can reserve a small pool of low-latency workers (num_tokens concurrency) that accept single-shot requests with minimal batching and a separate pool for high-throughput background traffic. The smart routing policy sends requests by priority.
[05:02] Marco: How aggressive is continuous batching wait window? If we set queue_wait_ms to 12 ms, won't that add to p95?
[05:10] Lena: It does add up, but the trick is to tune it in tandem with small worker pools for low-latency traffic. For example, background pool queue_wait_ms = 12 ms, low-latency pool = 1-2 ms or disabled batching. Then p95 for critical calls stays low.
[05:28] Aisha: Any guidance on scheduling knobs for on-prem? We control number of workers, GPUs per pod, and we can tune kernel selection.
[05:38] Lena: For on-prem with A100-80GB, we recommend: GPU partitioning with MIG profiles if you need multi-model tenancy; otherwise full GPU for single-model gives best throughput. Set per-worker max_concurrent_sequences to around 8-12 depending on model memory; set max_num_seqs to 48-64 for large models if you have homogeneous short requests, otherwise favor max_tokens_per_batch=24k-40k. Also, set queue_wait_ms adaptive: 6 ms base, up to 20 ms under high load.
[06:10] Marco: We also have network serialization overhead between model and routing. Any tips?
[06:16] Lena: Batch locality matters — prefer co-locating the router and runtime to avoid RPC overhead, or use gRPC with large keepalive windows. Also, enable kernel-level fused attention kernels for long seqs; they cut per-token time significantly. We'll share kernel recommendations in the spreadsheet.
[06:34] Samir: I'll drop the benchmark sheet link in the notes — it has profiles, recommended knobs, and a harness. https://redwood.app/benchmarks/neptune-throughput.xlsx
[06:44] Dana: Nice. We'll run the harness. A question on KV cache: if we shard KV by client id, does that increase memory duplication?
[06:54] Lena: Good catch — per-client KV improves cache hit for conversational flows but can increase memory if you keep many clients warm. Hybrid approach: per-route windowing where active clients retain KV and idle ones are compacted. Also use compressed kv representation with quantized keys when supported.
[07:10] Marco: Are there metrics we should surface to make tuning decisions?
[07:15] Lena: Yes — per-worker queue depth, average wait_ms, batch fill ratio, per-batch token count, KV cache size per-client, eviction count, and per-token p50/p95 latency. Redwood's console exposes these, but you can also export logs for offline analysis.
[07:35] Aisha: You mentioned scheduler trace — can your SEs join a run?
[07:40] Samir: Absolutely. Lena said she'd join. We'll schedule a 3-hour run where we test mixed traffic.
[07:50] Marco: On quantization — we tried 4-bit and saw output artifacts on long summaries. Is that common?
[07:56] Lena: It can happen. 4-bit often needs extra calibration or quant-aware fine-tuning. For long contexts it's more likely to drift. If cost/memory is critical, try 8-bit first and compare. In the bench sheet we'll include quality regression thresholds.
[08:12] Dana: Do you have an example config snippet for k8s pods and the scheduler flags?
[08:18] Lena: Yes, we'll include a sample. Key flags: --scheduler.max_num_seqs=48, --scheduler.max_tokens_per_batch=32768, --scheduler.queue_wait_ms=8, --worker.max_concurrent_sequences=10, --kv.eviction_policy=LRU-window, --quant.mode=8bit. We'll paste it in the shared doc.
[08:41] Priya (joining): Sorry, late. Quick question on security — if we enable KV cache sharding, does that change data residency or encryption controls?
[08:50] Samir: No, KV cache stays in-memory on your nodes for on-prem. We never persist unencrypted KV to disk unless configured; for private deployments you manage KMS keys. We'll send the on-prem security checklist and SOC2/ISO docs: https://redwood.app/security.pdf
[09:10] Marco: We're also concerned about multi-tenant noisy neighbors. If one client spikes with long sequences, how do we enforce fairness?
[09:20] Lena: You can enable per-client rate limits and per-route quotas. Also implement soft preemption: long-running sequences can be throttled or moved to a lower-priority pool. Another option is to allocate tokens-per-second budgets per client so bursts don't blow up the KV cache.
[09:40] Aisha: Let's talk measurable targets: we'd like to reduce p95 latency for chat from ~680 ms to <300 ms at 500 QPS mixed traffic, and increase throughput by 2.5x under background summarization. Are these realistic?
[09:56] Lena: Potentially yes with a combination of token-based batching, separating low-latency pools, and enabling optimized kernels + 8-bit quant. The bench run will quantify.
[10:10] Samir: We'll propose benchmark scenarios: steady state 500 QPS chat (80% short), bursty 1k QPS for 2 minutes, mixed background summarization with longer seqs. We'll also run a KV eviction stress test.
[10:28] Marco: After benchmarks, what config changes are non-disruptive? Can we change scheduler knobs without redeploying pods?
[10:34] Lena: Many knobs are dynamic — queue_wait_ms and max_tokens_per_batch can be tuned at runtime via the config API. Others like worker concurrency may require rolling restarts. We'll mark which are dynamic in the sheet.
[10:45] Dana: One more thing — how do we measure packing efficiency?
[10:50] Lena: Batch fill ratio and average tokens per-batch are the primary metrics. Also compute wasted slots = max_num_seqs - actual_seqs per batch over time. We can generate a histogram in the console.
[11:02] Aisha: Are there known regressions for quantized kernels on certain ops?
[11:08] Lena: Some ops like rotary embeddings or specialized attention variants may not yet have stable 4-bit kernels; we document model-specific notes in the bench sheet.
[11:20] Samir: Ok, let's recap next steps and owners. I'll send the benchmark spreadsheet and a suggested initial config. Lena will join the run and capture KV and scheduler traces. Marco will run the harness and share logs. Dana will provide sample prompts. We'll reconvene after data looks good to plan a pilot.
[11:40] Marco: Sounds good. Any follow-up on licensing or Dedicated vs Private?
[11:46] Samir: We'll include Dedicated capacity vs on-prem cost comparison in the notes — but for now the focus is tuning the existing on-prem deployment.
[11:55] Aisha: Thanks all.
[12:00] (call ends)

Notes: audio transcript shows occasional mis-heard words (e.g., "K-V cash" for KV cache, "max num sex" instead of max_num_seqs in auto-caption). Shared artifacts: benchmark spreadsheet (https://redwood.app/benchmarks/neptune-throughput.xlsx), security docs (https://redwood.app/security.pdf).
